preamble: Languages that lack the voiceless dental fricative [θ] but contrast aspirated and unaspirated stops typically map it onto the aspirated stop [tʰ] (dental [t̪ʰ] in Indo-Aryan) when adapting English words. The aspirated stop preserves the noisy, turbulent release of the fricative, which is why English /θ/ and English /t/ are kept apart: Hindi and Thai render English t with an unaspirated stop but th with an aspirated one.
phoneticEffects: Fortition, Stopping, Addition of Aspiration, Loanword Adaptation

examples.note: English /θ/ becomes the aspirated dental stop थ, while English /t/ becomes the unaspirated retroflex ट; the Urdu spelling تَھرْما مِیٹَر shows the same aspirated reflex.
North Indian speakers substitute the aspirated voiceless dental plosive for /θ/, a transfer from Indo-Aryan first languages.

examples.to: เทอร์โมมิเตอร์ /tʰɤː˧.moː˧.mi˦˥.tɤː˥˩/ 'thermometer'
examples.note: English th is written with aspirated ท /tʰ/, while the English /t/ of '-meter' is rendered with unaspirated ต /t/.
